title: A Unifying Review of Deep and Shallow Anomaly Detection
authors: Lukas Ruff, Jacob R. Kauffmann, Robert A. Vandermeulen, Grégoire Montavon, Wojciech Samek, Marius Kloft, Thomas G. Dietterich, Klaus-Robert Müller
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE, vol. 109, no. 5, pp. 756-795
key_claim: Unifies density, one-class and reconstruction-based AD. Every AD method encodes an assumption about what 'normal' is (concentration assumption: normal data lie in a low-volume region, anomalies elsewhere); the unsupervised setting assumes training data are (almost) all normal, and the semi-supervised / supervised settings are separate problem settings. Reconstruction error is a score only for anomalies that lie off the learned manifold.
supports_our_finding: Frames all four regimes we compare (contaminated unsupervised, one-class, latent-distance, supervised). Contaminated AE at chance = violated 'majority is normal' assumption; DataReplay below chance = anomaly on the normal manifold.
how_to_cite_it_in_our_paper: Background section: 'We follow the taxonomy of Ruff et al. [C01]; reconstruction-based detectors assume anomalies lie off the manifold of the training data, an assumption our GridSybil-majority training set and DataReplay attack both violate.'
verified_via: Web search this session: DOI, volume/pages, author list confirmed (arXiv 2009.11732 page + IEEE listing). Key-claim wording is a summary from the paper's known content, not quoted from a page fetched this session — check section numbers before quoting.

title: Deep One-Class Classification
authors: Lukas Ruff, Robert Vandermeulen, Nico Goernitz, Lucas Deecke, Shoaib Ahmed Siddiqui, Alexander Binder, Emmanuel Müller, Marius Kloft
key_claim: Deep SVDD trains a network with an anomaly-detection objective (minimum-volume hypersphere around normal data) instead of reusing reconstruction error; the one-class setting assumes the training set is normal.
supports_our_finding: Standard one-class baseline a reviewer will ask about; defines the benign-only regime our one-class AE belongs to. Distance-to-centre in latent space is the same idea as our Mahalanobis-on-z score.
how_to_cite_it_in_our_paper: Related work / limitations: 'We evaluate reconstruction and a latent-distance score; a learned one-class objective such as Deep SVDD [C02] is not tested.'

title: Deep Semi-Supervised Anomaly Detection
authors: Lukas Ruff, Robert A. Vandermeulen, Nico Görnitz, Alexander Binder, Emmanuel Müller, Klaus-Robert Müller, Marius Kloft
key_claim: Deep SAD generalises Deep SVDD to use a small set of labeled samples; reports equal or better results than shallow, hybrid and deep competitors even with little labeled data.
evidence_type: method paper + image and classic AD benchmarks
supports_our_finding: Frames the gap between our label-free detectors (0.48-0.74) and supervised models (0.93): a few labels are known to change the problem. Motivates a few-label follow-up.
how_to_cite_it_in_our_paper: Discussion: 'The large supervised / unsupervised gap is consistent with the semi-supervised AD literature, where a few labeled anomalies help strongly [C03, C10, C12].'

title: Do Deep Generative Models Know What They Don't Know?
authors: Eric Nalisnick, Akihiro Matsukawa, Yee Whye Teh, Dilan Gorur, Balaji Lakshminarayanan
area: failure of likelihood models on out-of-distribution data
key_claim: Flows, VAEs and autoregressive models trained on CIFAR-10 assign higher likelihood to SVHN than to their own training data; density estimates of deep generative models should not be trusted to flag out-of-distribution inputs.
supports_our_finding: The canonical 'below chance' anomaly result. Direct precedent for DataReplay AUROC 0.39 (replayed trajectories get lower error than benign test) and Mahalanobis 0.31-0.34 in the contaminated setting.
how_to_cite_it_in_our_paper: Results (DataReplay): 'A detector that scores anomalies as more normal than normal data is a known failure of generative novelty scores [C04, C06, C28]; we report an instance with a causal explanation (the attack replays genuine trajectories).'
verified_via: Web search this session: arXiv 1810.09136, ICLR 2019 poster page, author list, abstract findings.

title: Memorizing Normality to Detect Anomaly: Memory-Augmented Deep Autoencoder for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
authors: Dong Gong, Lingqiao Liu, Vuong Le, Budhaditya Saha, Moussa Reda Mansour, Svetha Venkatesh, Anton van den Hengel
key_claim: States the problem explicitly: an autoencoder sometimes 'generalizes' so well that it also reconstructs anomalies well, so anomalies are missed; proposes a memory module (MemAE) to limit this.
evidence_type: method paper motivated by a stated failure mode; image / video benchmarks
supports_our_finding: The most cited one-sentence statement of why our one-class AE misses DataReplay and (partly) GridSybil: low reconstruction error on anomalies.
how_to_cite_it_in_our_paper: Introduction and results: 'Autoencoders are known to reconstruct some anomalies as well as normal data [C05, C06].'

authors: Sangwoong Yoon, Yung-Kyun Noh, Frank Chongwoo Park

supports_our_finding: Gives the name and mechanism for our DataReplay / GridSybil reconstruction results.
how_to_cite_it_in_our_paper: Results: 'This is an instance of outlier reconstruction [C06].'

title: Improving Reconstruction Autoencoder Out-of-distribution Detection with Mahalanobis Distance
authors: Taylor Denouden, Rick Salay, Krzysztof Czarnecki, Vahdat Abdelzad, Buu Phan, Sachin Vernekar
key_claim: Reconstruction error alone is not a sufficient novelty score; adding the Mahalanobis distance between the encoded sample and the mean of the encoded training set often improves over reconstruction alone.
supports_our_finding: Source of the Mahalanobis-on-latent score we test. Our result is the opposite sign under contamination (0.31-0.34) and no gain in the one-class setting (0.51 GridSybil vs 0.74 reconstruction): the score needs clean, unimodal normal data.
how_to_cite_it_in_our_paper: Method: 'Following [C07] we also score by Mahalanobis distance in the latent space.' Results: 'Unlike [C07], it did not improve on reconstruction error.'

title: Anomaly Detection with Robust Deep Autoencoders
authors: Chong Zhou, Randy C. Paffenroth
key_claim: A standard autoencoder trained on data that contains outliers learns to reconstruct them; the Robust Deep Autoencoder splits the input into a part the AE reconstructs and a sparse outlier part (Robust PCA idea), i.e. no clean training set is assumed.
supports_our_finding: Early anchor for 'AE trained on contaminated data fits the contamination' — our mixed benign + attack autoencoders at AUROC 0.48.
how_to_cite_it_in_our_paper: Results (contaminated AE): 'That autoencoders fit anomalies present in the training set is known [C08, C09]; robust variants assume the anomalies are sparse, which a 64% attack share violates.'

title: Latent Outlier Exposure for Anomaly Detection with Contaminated Data
authors: Chen Qiu, Aodong Li, Marius Kloft, Maja Rudolph, Stephan Mandt
key_claim: Unsupervised AD usually assumes clean training data; unlabeled anomalies in the training set degrade the detector. LOE infers normal / anomalous labels jointly with the model and improves several backbones on image, tabular (30 datasets) and video data.
supports_our_finding: Modern anchor for the contamination effect. The literature studies contamination as a minority; we have an attack majority (64%), where 'normal' is redefined rather than merely blurred.
how_to_cite_it_in_our_paper: Related work: 'Contamination studies [C09, C10] consider small anomaly ratios (to be checked against the paper's tables); in VeReMi-Extension Sybil folders the attack is the majority class.'
verified_via: Web search this session: PMLR page, volume/pages, authors, abstract. The contamination ratios used in the paper were not checked this session.

title: ADBench: Anomaly Detection Benchmark
authors: Songqiao Han, Xiyang Hu, Hailiang Huang, Mingqi Jiang, Yue Zhao
area: realistic benchmark of AD under different supervision
key_claim: 30 algorithms × 57 datasets, studied by level of supervision, anomaly type, and noisy / corrupted data. Reported takeaways (from the paper body, not confirmed from a fetched page this session): no unsupervised method is statistically better than the others; a small amount of labels lets semi-supervised methods beat unsupervised ones; the best unsupervised method depends on the anomaly type.
supports_our_finding: Supports (a) the supervised / unsupervised gap, (b) 'detectability depends on the anomaly type' — our per-attack split (DoSRandom 0.97, GridSybil 0.74, DataReplay 0.39).
how_to_cite_it_in_our_paper: Discussion: 'As in ADBench [C10], which unsupervised score works depends on the anomaly type, and labels matter more than the detector.'

title: Current Time Series Anomaly Detection Benchmarks are Flawed and are Creating the Illusion of Progress
authors: Renjie Wu, Eamonn J. Keogh
venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering (online 2021, issue 2023); extended abstract at ICDE 2022
key_claim: Popular benchmarks suffer from four flaws — triviality (solvable with a one-line rule), unrealistic anomaly density, mislabeled ground truth, run-to-failure bias — so much reported progress may be illusory. Introduces the UCR Anomaly Archive.
